overview: The Kanien’kehá:ka, or Mohawk, are a continuing nation within the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Their communities have distinct local histories. This imported outline broadly follows the Mohawk Valley and St. Lawrence region; it does not mark one fixed border or imply that the nation ended in 1500.

periods.title: Farming villages and the Confederacy
periods.summary: Mohawk villages combined substantial homes, cultivated fields and regional political relationships.

periods.title: New pressures and changing settlements
periods.summary: Colonial wars and land loss reshaped communities, including settlement on the Grand River after 1784.

periods.title: Communities across borders
periods.summary: Mohawk communities sustain related identities through distinct governments, families and language work.

items.text: Mohawk clan identity traditionally passes from mother to child. The nation’s three clans are Bear, Wolf and Turtle, although Akwesasne also includes people from other Haudenosaunee clans. These relationships link families to responsibilities that extend beyond a single household.

At Otsungo, a Mohawk archaeological site not disturbed by plowing, a magnetometer detected buried hearths arranged in rows. Their pattern helped researchers identify longhouses even where wooden walls had vanished. The places people warmed themselves and cooked can outlast the house itself.

The New York State Museum explains longhouse construction using sturdy posts, bent rafters and sheets of bark. Bark lashings tightened as they dried. Building depended on choosing the right trees and harvesting materials at suitable seasons: the forest supplied both walls and fasteners.

The museum’s Mohawk Valley village reconstruction places corn, beans and squash fields near fortified homes. Archaeological interpretation joins buildings with the land needed to feed their occupants. A village was more than the houses inside its palisade; its food-growing landscape mattered too.

sections.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel

items.text: Akwesasne cornwashing baskets have a zigzag weave that helps remove the outer hulls from boiled corn during rinsing. Other baskets use an open weave to sift cornmeal, leaving large pieces for further grinding. A kitchen tool’s pattern can be beautiful and useful at the same time.

Black ash supplies strong, thin splints for basketry, but the trees face environmental threats. Akwesasne’s environmental task force collects seeds, records where they grew, dries them and stores them for planting. Protecting a craft can begin with caring for a tree decades before it becomes a basket.

For more than a century, many Kahnawà:ke men worked as ironworkers, often in the United States. The community’s account links this work to language change, as English became increasingly useful. Journeys for work connected life in Kahnawà:ke with distant construction sites.

Kahnawà:ke also maintains its own hospital, schools, social services, police service and media. These institutions are part of contemporary Mohawk life. A history card that stops at longhouses would miss children going to school, patients receiving care and a community managing everyday needs.

The 1784 Haldimand agreement provided land along the Grand River for Mohawk and other Six Nations people after losses during their British alliance in the American Revolution. Its provision extended six miles on each side of the river. This history belongs to particular relocated communities, not to every Mohawk family.

Akwesasne now crosses the Canada to United States border and the boundaries of Ontario, Quebec and New York. It has related but distinct traditional and elected governing bodies. The border divides jurisdictions, while family ties and community identity continue across it.

The Akwesasne Child Care Program greets families with “She:kon/Hello!” Its exact written Mohawk greeting means “Hello!” This is a contemporary language sample from a working community service, not an invented phrase assigned to the map’s 1492 date.

Kahnawà:ke’s language and cultural center began its adult immersion programme in 2002. The two-year course combines instruction with practical exercises and activities outside class. Adults study so that Mohawk can take a fuller place in conversations, families and community life.

ending.text: War, displacement and colonial policies changed Mohawk communities without ending the nation. Kahnawà:ke, Akwesasne and other communities continue their own political and cultural work. The 1500 map endpoint is a display interval, not an event in which Mohawk people disappeared.
